A Roth IRA is popular because, if you follow the rules, qualified withdrawals aren't taxed. But direct contributions to a Roth come with income limits. Earn above them, and you can't contribute directly. Conversions are different. The IRS says that regardless of your income, you may be able to convert money from a traditional IRA into a Roth IRA. So the backdoor is really two steps. First, a contribution to a traditional IRA that you don't deduct. Then, a conversion of that money into a Roth. It's reported on an IRS form, Form eighty-six-oh-six. Here's what the shortcut videos skip. The normal yearly contribution limits still apply, and you need taxable compensation to contribute at all. A conversion taxes any untaxed money that's being converted. And if you already have pre-tax money in traditional IRAs, the IRS looks at all of them together, so part of your conversion can be taxable, even though your new contribution wasn't deducted.
